subject: biology
title: Populations and communities
summary: How populations grow under exponential and logistic models, what carrying capacity and r and K strategies mean, and how communities are structured, change through succession and are measured for biodiversity.
body:
Ecologists want to know why some populations explode, others hold steady and others crash, and why some places hold many more species than others. Simple mathematical models of population growth, combined with ideas about community structure and succession, give us a way to predict these patterns. They are used every day in fisheries management, pest control, conservation planning and the recovery of land after fire or mining.

## Key ideas

### Populations and their parameters

A **population** is a group of individuals of the same species living in the same area at the same time. Its size (N) changes through four processes: births (B), deaths (D), immigration (I) and emigration (E). For a closed population (no movement in or out), the change in size over time is simply births minus deaths.

Ecologists express these as per capita rates. The **per capita birth rate** (b) is births per individual per unit time, and the **per capita death rate** (d) is deaths per individual per unit time. The difference is the **per capita rate of increase**, r = b − d. If r is positive the population grows; if it is zero the population is stable; if it is negative it declines.

**Population density** is the number of individuals per unit area or volume, and **dispersion** is the spacing pattern of individuals: clumped (around resources or social groups), uniform (often from territoriality) or random (when individuals do not affect one another).

### Exponential growth

When resources are unlimited, r stays constant no matter how big the population becomes. This gives **exponential growth**, described by:

`dN/dt = rN`

Here dN/dt is the rate of change of population size. Because the growth rate is proportional to N, the bigger the population, the faster it grows, producing a J-shaped curve. Integrating gives the population size at any time t:

`Nₜ = N₀eʳᵗ`

where N₀ is the starting size and e ≈ 2.718. When r takes its highest possible value for a species under ideal conditions, it is called the **intrinsic rate of increase** (r_max). A useful result is the **doubling time**, t_d = ln 2 / r ≈ 0.693 / r.

Exponential growth is seen in the short term when a species colonises a new habitat or recovers from a crash, such as rabbits after their introduction to Australia. It cannot continue indefinitely because resources always run out.

### Logistic growth and carrying capacity

The **carrying capacity** (K) is the maximum population size that a particular environment can support over the long term, set by limiting resources such as food, water, nesting sites or space. The **logistic growth model** adds a term that slows growth as N approaches K:

`dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K`

The fraction (K − N)/K is the proportion of carrying capacity still unused. When N is tiny, this fraction is close to 1 and growth is nearly exponential. When N = K, the fraction is 0 and growth stops. The result is an S-shaped (sigmoid) curve.

The population growth rate (dN/dt) is greatest at N = K/2, where it equals rK/4. Below K/2 there are too few individuals reproducing; above K/2 the shortage of resources slows growth. This is the basis of the idea of **maximum sustainable yield** in fisheries: harvesting a stock held near K/2 removes the most individuals per year without driving it down.

The logistic model assumes that each individual added reduces growth by the same amount and that the population responds instantly. Real populations often overshoot K and oscillate because of time lags (for example, between food shortage and reduced births).

### Density-dependent and density-independent factors

**Density-dependent factors** have a stronger effect per individual as density rises: competition for food, disease spread, predation and build-up of toxic waste. These are the factors that create a carrying capacity and regulate populations. **Density-independent factors** affect the same proportion of individuals regardless of density, for example a flood, frost or bushfire. They can cause large fluctuations but cannot by themselves hold a population near a stable size.

### r and K strategies

Life histories are sometimes placed on a continuum. **r-selected species** are favoured in unstable or uncrowded environments where rapid growth pays off: they mature early, produce many small offspring, give little parental care and are often short-lived (many annual weeds, insects). **K-selected species** are favoured in stable, crowded environments near carrying capacity, where competitive ability matters: they mature late, produce few large offspring, invest heavily in each and are long-lived (elephants, albatrosses, many large trees). Most species have a mix of traits, so the r–K scheme is a useful simplification rather than a strict classification.

### Community structure

A **community** is all the populations of different species that live and interact in an area. Its structure is described by:

- **Species richness** — the number of species present.
- **Species evenness** (relative abundance) — how equally individuals are spread among the species.
- **Trophic structure** — feeding relationships, from producers to primary, secondary and tertiary consumers, shown as food chains and food webs. Energy transfer between trophic levels is inefficient (roughly 10% passes on), which limits the length of food chains.
- **Dominant species** — the most abundant species or those with the highest biomass.
- **Keystone species** — species with an effect on community structure far larger than their abundance would suggest. A classic example is a predatory sea star whose removal from rocky shores allowed mussels to take over and species richness to fall.
- **Foundation species** (ecosystem engineers) — species that create or change habitat, such as corals or kelp.

### Succession and disturbance

**Ecological succession** is the change in species composition of a community over time after a disturbance. **Primary succession** starts on ground with no soil, such as new volcanic rock or land exposed by a retreating glacier. **Pioneer species** such as lichens and mosses arrive first, weather rock and add organic matter, slowly forming soil. **Secondary succession** occurs where a community has been removed but the soil remains, for example after fire or abandoned farming; it is much faster because seeds, roots and soil organisms are already present.

Early species can help later ones (**facilitation**), hinder them (**inhibition**) or have no effect (**tolerance**). The older idea of a single fixed **climax community** has been softened: disturbance is frequent, and many communities are a shifting mosaic. The **intermediate disturbance hypothesis** proposes that richness is highest at moderate levels of disturbance, because too little disturbance lets dominant competitors exclude others and too much allows only a few tolerant species to persist. Many Australian plant communities depend on fire for regeneration.

### Measuring biodiversity

Richness alone ignores evenness. Two diversity indices combine both:

**Simpson's index of diversity**:

`D = 1 − Σn(n − 1) / N(N − 1)`

where n is the number of individuals of each species and N is the total number of individuals. D ranges from 0 (no diversity) towards 1 (high diversity). It is the probability that two individuals picked at random belong to different species.

**Shannon index**:

`H = −Σpᵢ ln pᵢ`

where pᵢ is the proportion of individuals in species i. H increases with both richness and evenness. Evenness can be expressed as E = H / ln S, where S is species richness.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: exponential and logistic calculations

A population of 50 wallabies is released on a predator-free island. Under ideal conditions r = 0.4 per year.

(a) Predict the population after 5 years if growth is exponential.

- Formula: Nₜ = N₀eʳᵗ
- Substitute: Nₜ = 50 × e^(0.4 × 5) = 50 × e² = 50 × 7.389
- Nₜ ≈ 369 wallabies.

(b) The island's carrying capacity is K = 1000. Calculate dN/dt when N = 200.

- Formula: dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K
- Substitute: dN/dt = 0.4 × 200 × (1000 − 200)/1000 = 80 × 0.8
- dN/dt = 64 wallabies per year.

(c) At what population size is growth fastest, and how fast is it?

- At N = K/2 = 500, dN/dt = rK/4 = 0.4 × 1000 / 4 = 100 wallabies per year.

Note that at N = 200 the exponential model would predict 0.4 × 200 = 80 per year, so the logistic model already shows a 20% reduction.

### Example 2: comparing diversity of two sites

A student counts four species of beetle in two pitfall-trap sites.

| Species | Site 1 | Site 2 |
|---|---|---|
| A | 10 | 37 |
| B | 10 | 1 |
| C | 10 | 1 |
| D | 10 | 1 |
| Total (N) | 40 | 40 |

Both sites have a richness of 4. Calculate Simpson's index for each.

Site 1: Σn(n − 1) = 4 × (10 × 9) = 360; N(N − 1) = 40 × 39 = 1560.
D = 1 − 360/1560 = 1 − 0.231 = 0.769.

Site 2: Σn(n − 1) = 37 × 36 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 1332.
D = 1 − 1332/1560 = 1 − 0.854 = 0.146.

Interpretation: Site 1 is far more diverse even though richness is identical, because its individuals are spread evenly. Site 2 is dominated by species A. A sound conclusion also notes sample limitations: one trapping session, at one time of year, with equal effort.

## Common mistakes

- Confusing r (the per capita rate) with dN/dt (the growth rate of the whole population). A population can have a high r yet a small dN/dt if N is small.
- Thinking growth is fastest at carrying capacity. In the logistic model growth stops at K and is fastest at K/2.
- Treating carrying capacity as a fixed property of a species. K depends on the environment and can change with seasons, drought or habitat loss.
- Using species richness as if it were diversity. Evenness matters too.
- Calling any slow-growing species K-selected. The r–K scheme describes suites of traits and is a continuum.

## Exam tips

- Show the formula, substitution and units (individuals per unit time) in every growth calculation; marks are often given for each step.
- When interpreting a growth curve, name the phase (lag, exponential, deceleration, plateau) and link it to a cause such as resource limitation.
- For diversity data questions, calculate the index, then explain the result in terms of richness and evenness, and comment on sampling.
- Be ready to classify a factor as density-dependent or density-independent and justify it.

## Tips to remember

- **"J for Jump, S for Stop"** (made-up memory trick): exponential growth (dN/dt = rN) jumps up in a J-shaped curve while resources are unlimited; logistic growth (dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K) bends into an S and stops at carrying capacity K.
- **The (K − N)/K term is the "empty seats" fraction**: think of K as the seats in a cinema. When almost empty, nearly every seat is free and growth is near-exponential; when full (N = K), no seats are left and growth is zero.
- **Halfway is the sweet spot**: logistic growth is fastest at N = K/2 (where dN/dt = rK/4), which is why maximum sustainable yield aims to hold a fish stock near K/2, not at K.
- **Density-dependent = depends on crowding** (competition, disease, predation, waste) and regulates populations; **density-independent** = a flood, frost or bushfire that hits the same proportion whatever the density.
- **r = "rapid and many", K = "Kare and few"** (made-up memory trick): r-selected species mature early with many small offspring and little care; K-selected species mature late with few large offspring and lots of parental care. Remember it is a continuum.
- **Primary succession starts from bare rock, secondary from bare soil**: secondary is faster because seeds, roots and soil organisms are already there. Self-check on diversity: richness counts species; Simpson's and Shannon indices also reward evenness.

## Key terms

- **Population** — individuals of one species in one area at one time.
- **Per capita rate of increase (r)** — per capita birth rate minus per capita death rate.
- **Exponential growth** — growth at a constant per capita rate, giving a J-shaped curve.
- **Carrying capacity (K)** — the largest population an environment can support long term.
- **Logistic growth** — growth that slows as N approaches K, giving an S-shaped curve.
- **Density-dependent factor** — a factor whose effect per individual increases with density.
- **r-selected / K-selected** — life history suites favoured in uncrowded versus crowded environments.
- **Keystone species** — a species with a disproportionately large effect on its community.
- **Succession** — change in community composition over time after disturbance.
- **Simpson's index** — a diversity index giving the probability that two random individuals are different species.

## Summary

- Population change depends on births, deaths, immigration and emigration; r = b − d.
- Exponential growth (dN/dt = rN) occurs only while resources are unlimited.
- Logistic growth (dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K) levels off at carrying capacity and is fastest at K/2.
- r- and K-selected species differ in maturity, offspring number, parental care and lifespan.
- Communities are described by richness, evenness, trophic structure and key species; they change through primary and secondary succession.
- Diversity indices such as Simpson's and Shannon's combine richness and evenness.

questions.prompt: In the logistic growth equation dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K, what does the term (K − N)/K represent?

options.A: The per capita birth rate of the population
options.B: The proportion of the carrying capacity that is still unused
options.C: The number of individuals that will die in the next time interval
options.D: The intrinsic rate of increase under ideal conditions

questions.explanation: (K − N)/K is the fraction of carrying capacity not yet filled; it falls from about 1 to 0 as N rises to K, slowing growth. D is tempting because r appears in the equation, but r is a separate term, not this fraction.

questions.prompt: Which set of traits is most typical of an r-selected species?

options.A: Late maturity, few large offspring, extensive parental care
options.B: Long lifespan, repeated breeding, strong competitive ability
options.C: Populations held close to carrying capacity in stable habitats
options.D: Early maturity, many small offspring, little parental care

questions.explanation: r-selected species are favoured where rapid population growth pays off, so they breed early and produce many cheap offspring. A describes a K-selected species, a common mix-up when students remember only that r and K are opposites.

questions.prompt: According to the logistic model, why is the population growth rate (dN/dt) greatest when N = K/2?

options.A: Below K/2 there are few individuals breeding, and above K/2 resource limitation increasingly reduces per capita growth
options.B: The per capita rate of increase is at its maximum value at K/2
options.C: Density-independent factors stop acting at K/2
options.D: Births equal deaths at K/2, so the population is stable

questions.explanation: dN/dt is the product of N and the per capita growth rate; this product peaks halfway to K. B is tempting, but per capita growth is highest when N is near zero, not at K/2. Births equal deaths at K, not K/2.

questions.prompt: A pine plantation is clear-felled and then abandoned. Over 40 years native shrubs and then eucalypts re-establish. This is best described as:

options.A: Primary succession, because new species colonise the site
options.B: Exponential growth of the plant community
options.C: Secondary succession, because soil and its seed bank remained after the disturbance
options.D: Primary succession, because the original pine community was destroyed

questions.explanation: Secondary succession follows a disturbance that removes the community but leaves the soil. Primary succession (A, D) starts on bare substrate with no soil; removing the plants does not make it primary.

questions.prompt: Two sites each contain 5 species and 100 individuals. Site X has 20 individuals of each species; Site Y has 96 of one species and 1 of each of the others. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Both sites have the same diversity because richness is identical
options.B: Site Y has higher diversity because it contains a dominant species
options.C: Site Y has a higher Simpson's index because one species is very abundant
options.D: Site X has higher diversity because its individuals are spread evenly among species

questions.explanation: Diversity indices combine richness and evenness, so with equal richness the more even site (X) is more diverse. A is the common error of treating richness as diversity.

questions.prompt: A bacterial population of 200 cells grows exponentially with r = 0.1 per day. Approximately how many cells will there be after 10 days?
questions.explanation: Nₜ = N₀eʳᵗ = 200 × e^(0.1 × 10) = 200 × e¹ = 200 × 2.718 ≈ 544. C comes from adding 10% of the original 200 each day (simple, not exponential, growth), and B assumes one doubling.

questions.prompt: A kangaroo population has r = 0.2 per year and K = 5000. What is the population growth rate when N = 1000?
questions.explanation: dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K = 0.2 × 1000 × (4000/5000) = 200 × 0.8 = 160 per year. A is the exponential answer (rN) that ignores the logistic term, and B uses N/K instead of (K − N)/K.

questions.prompt: A population of an invasive weed grows exponentially with r = 0.035 per year. What is its doubling time?
questions.explanation: t_d = ln 2 / r = 0.693 / 0.035 = 19.8 years. C is 1/r (forgetting ln 2), and D is 2/r.
